hints: Focus on what the word free-radical tells you about how bonds must break to start the reaction.
Remember initiation is UV light splitting $\text{Cl}_2$ into two identical $\text{Cl}\bullet$ radicals, which tells you the fission type.
Look at the first propagation step where $\text{Cl}\bullet$ removes H from $\text{CH}_4$, then ask what carbon fragment is left behind as a radical.
walkthrough:
**Recall How Radicals Form**

Free radicals form when a covalent bond breaks evenly, with one electron going to each atom. This is called homolytic fission.

Initiation equation:
$$\text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{UV light}} 2\text{Cl}\bullet$$

**Follow The First Propagation Step**

A chlorine radical is very reactive, so it attacks methane and steals a hydrogen atom to form $\text{HCl}$. The methane loses one H but keeps one unpaired electron.

Propagation step 1:
$$\text{Cl}\bullet + \text{CH}_4 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\bullet + \text{HCl}$$

**Check The Second Propagation Step**

The new methyl radical then attacks another $\text{Cl}_2$ molecule to make the product and regenerate $\text{Cl}\bullet$ to keep the chain going.

Propagation step 2:
$$\text{CH}_3\bullet + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{Cl} + \text{Cl}\bullet$$

**Put The Row Together**

Initiation needs homolytic fission, not heterolytic fission which would make ions. A propagation stage clearly produces $\text{CH}_3\bullet$. That combination matches only one row.

options.A: Homolytic fission is correct for initiation, but $\text{H}\bullet$ is not produced in propagation. The $\text{Cl}\bullet$ removes H from $\text{CH}_4$ to give $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{CH}_3\bullet$, so no free hydrogen radical appears.
options.B: Initiation is homolytic fission of $\text{Cl-Cl}$ to give two $\text{Cl}\bullet$ radicals. The first propagation step $\text{Cl}\bullet + \text{CH}_4 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\bullet + \text{HCl}$ produces the methyl radical $\text{CH}_3\bullet$. Both columns are correct.
options.C: Heterolytic fission is wrong. That would split electrons unevenly to give $\text{Cl}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$, which happens in polar reactions, not in free-radical substitution. $\text{H}\bullet$ is also not a propagation product.
options.D: $\text{CH}_3\bullet$ is indeed a propagation radical, but heterolytic fission is wrong for initiation. Students who confuse radical formation with ionic formation often pick this trap.
